explanations.2001-portuguese-local-elections--2002-po: Nothing obliged Guterres to resign: he had a legislature running to 2003 and the local result changed no seat in the Assembly. He resigned on the night, in his own phrase to avoid the country falling into a political swamp, and the president dissolved the Assembly in December for an election in March. The election of 2002 exists because of a ballot that was not about it, and the atlas keeps the edge as `caused` because the chain has no other link in it: local defeat, resignation, dissolution, early election, all inside three months.
explanations.2002-portuguese-legislative-election--20: The legislature this election returned should have run to 2006 and ran to 2005, and the reason is inside it. Durão Barroso left the government he led for the European Commission in July 2004; Santana Lopes took over without going back to the country; and in November President Sampaio dismissed the government — using, for the only time in the democratic period, the power to dissolve against a majority that still had one. The early election of February 2005 is the direct consequence of a prime minister leaving mid-term, and that is what the edge argues.
explanations.2003-invasion-of-iraq--iraqi-insurgency-: The article, of what the invasion left behind: "More serious for the post-war state of Iraq was the looting of cached weaponry and ordnance which fueled the subsequent insurgency. As many as 250,000 tons of explosives were unaccounted for by October 2004." `enabled` and not `caused`: what the article puts on the invasion is the means — the unguarded depots — and not the motive. The same article makes the same kind of claim about the force level, which "proved to be short-sighted ... due to the requirement for a much larger force to combat the irregular Iraqi forces in the Iraqi insurgency". Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.2005-portuguese-legislative-election--20: Holding the referendum again was a Socialist commitment in the 2005 campaign, made in as many words, and the absolute majority is what made it a decision rather than a negotiation: the Assembly approved the question, the president called it and the ballot was held on 11 February 2007. The atlas argues the direct line because there is no other: the question had been settled in the negative in 1998, no party had put it back since, and the government elected in 2005 put it back because it had said it would.

The English article on the election of 2009 reads it against the one before: the vote came after four years under a majority government of the Socialist Party, and the Socialists, led by then prime minister José Sócrates, won the largest number of votes and seats but failed to repeat the overall majority they had obtained in 2005, losing eight per cent of the vote and twenty-four seats.
explanations.2006-hezbollah-cross-border-raid--2006-l: The English article on the raid says that after Hezbollah ambushed the patrol and captured two soldiers, "Israel refused and launched a large-scale ground and air campaign across Lebanon in response to the Hezbollah raid. This marked the start of the 2006 Lebanon War." Wikidata gives the raid as the war's immediate cause (Q49104, P1478). The raid is also filed as part of the war, which is Wikidata's own P361 and a display fact; the edge is the separate claim that the campaign was a response to it.
explanations.2009-portuguese-legislative-election--tr: The request of April 2011 was made by a government that had resigned, to a parliament that had refused its fourth austerity package, in a market that had stopped lending to it. The election of 2009 is where the arithmetic comes from: a Socialist government forty-nine seats short of a majority, dependent on opponents who had every reason to withhold the votes and then to force an election. The edge is `precondition-of` rather than `caused` because the debt, the deficit and the sovereign crisis in the euro area would have been there whatever the Assembly looked like — what this election settled was that there would be no majority to meet them with.
explanations.2011-egyptian-revolution--2011-bahraini-: The same sentence names Egypt beside Tunisia — “inspired by the unrest of the 2011 Arab Spring and protests in Tunisia and Egypt” — and the Egyptian revolution is a record this atlas already holds. Two edges rather than one because the article names two protests and not a single source, and the atlas would be putting words in it by choosing between them.
explanations.2011-egyptian-revolution--2011-yemeni-re: The article gives the Egyptian revolution as a model the Yemeni opposition named: **"by February, opposition leader Tawakel Karman called for a 'Day of Rage' in the mold of mass nationwide demonstrations that helped to topple the government of Tunisia and put pressure on the government of President Hosni Mubarak in Egypt"**, and **"after Mubarak quit power in Egypt, demonstrators celebrating the revolution and calling for a similar uprising in Yemen were attacked by police and pro-Saleh tribesmen."** The infobox lists among the causes "inspiration from concurrent regional protests" and files the revolution under the Arab Spring, which this atlas does not hold as a record (deviation 975). `inspired` is the type for exactly this and the article supports no stronger one: the Yemeni protests began in January 2011 before Mubarak fell.
explanations.2011-egyptian-revolution--2013-egyptian-: The English article on the coup writes its background as the two years between: Mubarak resigned in February 2011 after eighteen days of mass demonstrations, the caretaker government approved an election law in July, a parliament was elected between December 2011 and January 2012, and Morsi won the presidential election of June 2012 to become the first democratically elected president of Egypt — the president the coup of 3 July 2013 removed.
explanations.2011-military-intervention-in-libya--sec: The article: "The battle marked the start of a United Nations-mandated military intervention in the conflict, with fighter jets from the French Air Force attacking and destroying several pro-Gaddafi units, forcing them to retreat", and, in § France intervenes: "at 4:45 pm, coalition intervention began as a French fighter jet fired on and destroyed several loyalist armored vehicles ... Admiral Mullen of the United States announced on 20 March, that the international coalition had stopped the regime's progression on Benghazi." `reacted-to` is the only one of the five that fits: the first strikes were flown against the column entering Benghazi that morning, so the intervention answers this battle rather than causing it or standing as its condition. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.2011-portuguese-legislative-election--20: Sócrates resigned the leadership on the night of the defeat, as he had resigned the government in March, and the party had to elect a successor within weeks. The ballot of 22 and 23 July exists for that reason and no other. The atlas keeps a party’s internal election as an event where something follows from it, and what follows from this one is the leadership that the primary of 2014 was called to end.
explanations.2011-portuguese-legislative-election--tr: A three-year adjustment programme has to be carried by a government that survives it, and Portugal's was: the coalition elected in June 2011 was still in office in May 2014 and it left the programme without the precautionary credit line, which was its own decision and not the lenders'. The atlas argues the political condition rather than the economics. The memorandum was signed by a caretaker government of a party that then lost; what this election supplied was a majority that had campaigned on carrying it out and had four years to do so.
explanations.2011-portuguese-socialist-party-leadersh: The primary of 2014 was a challenge to a sitting leader, and this is the ballot that made him one. Seguro had been elected in 2011 without a contest of this kind and had never been the party's candidate for prime minister; the open primary was the instrument found to settle both questions at once, and it could only have been aimed at the incumbency this election created. The edge is `precondition-of` rather than `caused`: what 2011 produced was the position that was challenged, not the challenge.
explanations.2011-south-sudanese-independence-referen: The English article on the civil war says the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005 created a Southern Sudan Autonomous Region run by the SPLM with a promise of a referendum on independence in 2011, and that **during the six years of autonomy the desire for independence kept the in-fighting within the SPLM in check**; in the referendum 98 per cent voted for independence and South Sudan became a state on 9 July 2011. The war broke out in December 2013 between the SPLM and the SPLM-IO. The article names what the referendum removed and does not call it the cause, which is why this is a precondition.
explanations.2012-malian-coup-d-etat--battle-of-kidal: The coup article makes the coup the reason the north fell: "Inspired in part by the diversion caused by the military coup, Tuareg rebels in the country's north launched incursions deeper into Mali, seizing towns and bases formerly held by government forces", and "As military forces were engaged in consolidating their hold on the capital, the rebels were able to push southward with little opposition." Kidal is the first of the three capitals that went, four days later. Enabled and not caused: the rebels were already besieging Kidal, and what the coup gave them was an army looking the other way. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.2012-tuareg-rebellion--2012-malian-coup-: The coup’s article gives the rebellion as the soldiers’ own grievance: it “began on 21 March that year, when mutinying Malian soldiers, displeased with the management of the Tuareg rebellion, attacked several locations in the capital Bamako, including the presidential palace, state television, and military barracks.”
explanations.2012-tuareg-rebellion--battle-of-gao--pr: The rebellion's own article puts the Battle of Gao at the end of what the rebellion left unsettled: "After the end of hostilities with the Malian Army, however, Tuareg nationalists and Islamists struggled to reconcile their conflicting visions for the intended new state. On 27 June, Islamists from the Movement for Oneness and Jihad in West Africa (MOJWA) clashed with the MNLA in the Battle of Gao". The Gao article says the same from its own side: "in early 2012 the MNLA and Islamist movements captured northern Mali. Tensions then started between the MNLA and Islamist movements over the use of sharia law within the territory." Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.2012-tuareg-rebellion--operation-barkhan: Barkhane’s own background is the northern Mali the rebellion opened and the Islamist groups that took it. The article reads: "As part of the fallout from the Libyan Civil War, instability in northern Mali caused by a Tuareg rebellion against the central Malian government was exploited by Islamist groups who gained control over the northern half of the country."
explanations.2014-portuguese-socialist-party-prime-mi: The arithmetic of October 2015 was there whoever led the Socialists: the PS, the Bloco, the PCP and the Greens held a majority of the seats between them. What was not there in any previous parliament was a Socialist leader willing to govern on written agreements with the two parties to his left, and to argue in public that the largest list does not automatically govern. Costa had said so during the primary and won it saying so. The edge argues the disposition and not the numbers, which is why it is `enabled` and why the atlas keeps the primary as an event at all.
explanations.2014-pro-russian-unrest-in-ukraine--war-: The article runs the one into the other. Its § Protests in the Donbas opens “Following the revolution, counter-revolutionary and pro-Russian protests began in parts of the Donbas” and, of 6 April, “demonstrators in Donetsk demanded a referendum on autonomy or accession to Russia”; six days later “unmarked pro-Russian militants seized the Donetsk headquarters of the Interior Ministry and two police stations without resistance”, which is where this record begins. `enabled`: the protests are the ground the armed seizures were made on and not an order to make them, and the lead gives the war’s own movers as “Russian-backed paramilitaries”.
explanations.2020-malian-coup-d-etat--2021-malian-cou: The second coup was made by the man the first one put in place, and the article says so: “Assimi Goïta, the head of the junta that led the 2020 Malian coup d’état, announced that N’daw and Ouane were stripped of their powers and that new elections would be held in 2022. It is the country’s third coup d’état in ten years, following the 2012 and 2020 military takeovers, with the latter having happened only nine months earlier.” The transitional government the 2020 coup created is what the 2021 coup deposed, so the first is a precondition of the second; the article does not say the first brought the second about, and the type is written to that.
explanations.2020-malian-coup-d-etat--moura-massacre-: The massacre's own § Background is a chain of three sentences from the coup to the force that carried the massacre out: France "announced after the 2020 Malian coup d'état their intention to gradually reduce the number of French forces and withdraw them from the country. Mali has since looked for other ways to acquire foreign help, and has received help from Wagner Group, a Russian private military company." The lead names Wagner, with the Malian army, as who carried the massacre out. Precondition and not cause: the article argues why those troops were in Mali, not why they killed. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.2021-malian-coup-d-etat--french-military: The article names both ends in one sentence and states the relation: "As a result of the 2021 Malian coup d'état, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the end of the operation and his intentions to remove troops incrementally." The operation is Operation Barkhane, which the same paragraph has just called "less successful than its predecessor"; the withdrawal this record is about is the withdrawal of it. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.2021-malian-coup-d-etat--kidal-offensive: The offensive's own lead makes the junta one of its two parties and dates that junta to the coup: "The offensive was part of a renewed conflict between the Malian junta that took power in 2021 and former Tuareg rebel groups that had signed the Algiers Agreement in 2015." § Background works the same ground: the CSP-PSD formed in April 2021, "just a month later" Goïta's coup took power, and "Goita and the CSP-PSD got off to a rocky start". Precondition and not cause: the article says the coup made the two parties what they were, not that it ordered the convoy north. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.2021-myanmar-coup-d-etat--myanmar-civil-: The English article of the war opens on the coup and gives it as what began the war: “The Myanmar civil war began following the military coup on 1 February 2021. The seizure of power triggered mass anti-coup demonstrations and a violent crackdown by the Tatmadaw (Myanmar armed forces), which significantly escalated the country’s longstanding insurgencies.” The insurgencies are older than the coup and the article says so; what it dates to February 2021 is the war.
explanations.2022-brazilian-general-election--2023-br: The English article of the attack gives the election as what the mob was answering: "Bolsonaro supporters alleged that the 2022 Brazilian general election suffered from widespread electoral fraud that caused Bolsonaro's loss. They claimed electronic voting machine malfunctions and deemed some voting patterns suspicious, and mistrusted election officials. The military helped oversee the election and found no signs of fraud." Its lead dates the attack to the week after the inauguration of the winner.
explanations.2022-brazilian-general-election--lula-re: The English article states the result plainly: "Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva received the majority of the votes in the second round and was elected president of Brazil for a third, non-consecutive term." The runoff of 30 October 2022 is what put him back in the Planalto on 1 January 2023.
explanations.2022-portuguese-social-democratic-party-: The ballot of 27 November was brought forward by a week for a reason: the president had dissolved the Assembly on 5 November and the party needed a candidate for prime minister before the campaign. That is what this election chose — not only a leader for the next two years but the name at the head of the largest opposition list on 30 January. The edge is `precondition-of` because the legislative election was already called when this one was held: what the party settled was who would fight it, not that it would happen.

The government of April 2024 is a Democratic Alliance government, and the alliance with the CDS was Montenegro's own reconstruction of a formula last used in 1980. He could make it because this ballot had given him the party two years earlier, with a mandate that included going back to a coalition his predecessor had refused. The edge is `precondition-of`: what put him in the prime minister's office was the election of March 2024, and what put him at the head of the list that won it was this.
explanations.2023-madeiran-regional-election--2024-ma: The snap election of May 2024 was caused by a corruption investigation and a resignation, not by the ballot of September 2023. What the 2023 ballot fixed was when it could happen: the constitution forbids the president from dissolving a legislative assembly within six months of its election, so between Albuquerque's resignation on 5 February and the dissolution on 27 March nothing could be done, and a region governed by a resigned cabinet waited seven weeks for a clock to run out. The edge argues that constraint, which is why it is `precondition-of`.
explanations.2024-madeiran-regional-election--2025-ma: The ballot of May 2024 returned the same party, the same leader and the same absence of a majority as the one eight months before it, in an assembly where the opposition had by then decided it would not tolerate him. The motion of censure approved in December is what the result made available and what the parties used; the dissolution and the election of 23 March 2025 followed within three months. An election that changes nothing in a chamber that has stopped supporting the government is a cause of the next election, and that is what this edge says.
explanations.battle-of-ajdabiya--first-gulf-of-sidra-: The offensive's own article dates itself from the battle: "It was mounted by anti-Gaddafi forces immediately after their victory in the Battle of Ajdabiya. The offensive was meant to have the rebel forces quickly reach Gaddafi's hometown of Sirte." `precondition-of`: taking Ajdabiya is what put the rebels back on the road west, and the article gives the offensive its own aim. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-bin-jawad--second-battle-of-be: Bin Jawad's § Aftermath makes the claim in its own words: "The Battle of Bin Jawad marked the end of the initial rebel offensive. Proving to be the high-water mark of the rebel offensive, it marked the end of the rebel advance westward at the time, and opened the way for a government counter-offensive that took pro-Gaddafi forces as far as the gates of Benghazi, before being pushed back by UN intervention." The counter-offensive reaching those gates is the second battle of Benghazi of 19 March. `enabled` and not `caused`: "opened the way for" is what the article says, and a counter-offensive has its own reasons. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-bin-jawad--second-battle-of-br: The Second Battle of Brega's article opens by saying what put the loyalists back outside Brega: "However, after the Battle of Bin Jawad and the Battle of Ra's Lanuf, government troops retook all of the lost territory and were once again threatening Brega by mid-March." The battle this atlas dates 13 to 15 March is the one that threat became. `precondition-of`: the article states the sequence and the ground it left behind, not an intent. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-diabaly--battle-of-ifoghas--pr: The other half of the same sentence: "After being defeated in January in the Battle of Konna and the Battle of Diabaly, the jihadists abandoned Timbuktu and retreated into the Adrar Tigharghar ... The French started quickly a pursuit". Two defeats are named and each is written as its own edge, because the article gives them equal weight and neither alone is what it says. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-diabaly--second-battle-of-gao-: Gao's § Prelude makes the advance on the city the next step of the same push: "A few days after taking the towns of Konna and Diabaly, the French and Malian forces continued their progress on Timbuktu and Gao", and then singles Diabaly out — "After the capture of Diabaly, the special forces advanced in Gao, the largest city in northern Mali". Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-gao--battle-of-in-delimane-201: The same sentence that opens the article names the lost city as what the fighting at Idelimane was an attempt to recover: "On November 16, MNLA forces launched an offensive to retake the city of Gao, but they came up against the Islamists forces of MUJAO and AQIM between Ansongo and Gao... the same day MUJAO attack elements of the MNLA in the village of Idelimane 80 kilometers from Ménaka, the last bastion of the MNLA." Precondition and not cause: Gao's loss is what the offensive was answering, and the article claims no more than that. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-gao--second-battle-of-menaka--: The Ménaka article states both halves in one sentence — that Gao had been the MNLA's base and was taken from it, and that the attack on Ménaka was the answer to the attempt to get it back: "On 16 November 2012, during the MNLA (Movement for the National Liberation of Azawad) failed offensive to reclaim its former city-base of Gao recently taken by Islamists groups, Islamists launch a counter-attack of their own targeted at the MNLA stronghold of Ménaka, north of Gao, the last bastion under MNLA control." Precondition and not cause: five months separate the two and the article gives the June battle as the standing situation the November attack was made in. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-gao--tagarangabotte-ambush--pr: The ambush is what the MNLA's attempt to undo the loss of Gao ran into: "On November 16, MNLA forces launched an offensive to retake the city of Gao, but they came up against the Islamists forces of MUJAO and AQIM between Ansongo and Gao. On the morning of the first day, Tuareg independence forces were successful in the Ambush of Tagarangabotte 50 kilometers east of Ansongo." The city the offensive set out to retake is the one the June battle took from the MNLA, which the Ménaka article at revision 1370736445 states in its own words: "its former city-base of Gao recently taken by Islamists groups". Precondition and not cause: the article says what the November fighting was for, not that the June battle brought it about. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-imenas--battle-of-tin-keraten-: Tin Keraten's own background opens on Imenas and carries the same column forward: "After the victory of the Battle of Iminenas, the French and Malian forces continued their war against the Islamist Jihadist coalition of MOJWA, AQIM, Ansar Dine and Al-Mulathamen", and then "The next target of the Franco-Malian forces was the wadi of Tin Keraten, located north-east of Imenas, 100 kilometers east of Gao." One force, one sweep east of Gao, and the second ground named as the next objective of the first — which is a continuation and not a date. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-in-delimane-2012--second-battl: The Ménaka article makes the victory at Idelimane the thing the attack on the town was launched from: "On 19 November, following its victory against the MNLA at the Battle of Idelimane, MUJAO continues its push and attacks the city of Menaka." The Idelimane article ends on the same sequence from its own side — "Next, the Battle of Ménaka followed" — and adds that the MNLA was routed there on 17 November with the loss of its force. Enabled and not caused: the article names the victory as what let the push go on, and does not say the battle at Idelimane brought the attack on Ménaka about. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-konna--battle-of-ifoghas--prec: The Ifoghas article says why the fighting moved to the mountains: "After being defeated in January in the Battle of Konna and the Battle of Diabaly, the jihadists abandoned Timbuktu and retreated into the Adrar Tigharghar, a mountain of the Adrar of Ifoghas in northeastern Mali, which has been their sanctuary for years. The French started quickly a pursuit". The defeat at Konna is half of what put them there. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-konna--operation-serval--cause: The article states the cause in one sentence: "However, the jihadist offensive in southern Mali provoked France's entry into the war. On January 11, the French army launched Operation Serval." Konna is that offensive — the same article calls the battle "among the first French engagements in their intervention in the Mali War". Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-ras-lanuf--battle-of-bin-jawad: Bin Jawad's own article dates the advance from Ras Lanuf and names the battle it came out of: "On 5 March 2011, following the Battle of Ra's Lanuf, rebel forces advanced along the Mediterranean coast and captured the town of Bin Jawad." The Second Battle of Brega's article says the same from further east: "Following that battle, rebel forces advanced along the Libyan Coastal Highway, taking the towns of Ra's Lanuf and Bin Jawad." `precondition-of` and not `caused`: taking Ras Lanuf is what put the rebel column on the coastal road west of it, which is a position and not a motive. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-ras-lanuf--second-battle-of-be: The article, § Aftermath: "After the battle the town was firmly in loyalist hands and government troops advanced further east taking the towns of Brega and Ajdabiya and reaching Benghazi." The loyalist recapture of Ras Lanuf on 11 March is the start of the advance that stood outside Benghazi eight days later. `precondition-of`: the article gives the advance its road and not its reason. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-sirte-2011--killing-of-muammar: The article's own lead: "The Battle of Sirte was the final and most decisive battle of the First Libyan Civil War, beginning when the National Liberation Army attacked the last remnants of the Libyan army still loyal to Muammar Gaddafi in his hometown and designated capital of Sirte ... Both Gaddafi and his son, Mutassim, were wounded and captured, then tortured and killed in custody less than an hour later." `caused` and not `precondition-of`: the capture happened inside this battle and the killing followed it within the hour, which is the article stating one thing bringing about the other and not a condition standing ready. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-timbuktu--second-battle-of-tim: The second battle's article gives the first its whole § Background, under {{Main articles|Battle of Timbuktu}}, and ends it on the link: "French forces expected a second attack on the city following the jihadist's failed first incursion. The French 1st Marine Infantry Regiment received reinforcements from the 92nd Infantry Regiment and the 126th Infantry Regiment." The first attack's failure is why the garrison the second met was the size it was. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-tripoli-2011--battle-of-bani-w: Bani Walid's § Background names what the advance on it followed: "Following the collapse of loyalist forces in Zawiya, Zliten and finally Tripoli in mid to late August, NLA forces advanced southwards from Misrata and Tarhuna towards the apparent pro-Gaddafi stronghold of Bani Walid." Of the three collapses it lists, Tripoli is the one this atlas holds — the Zawiya it means is the second battle of August and not the first, which is the one here. `precondition-of`: taking Tripoli freed the forces and the direction, and a stronghold under siege is a position. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-tripoli-2011--killing-of-muamm: The killing's article opens its account of what happened with the fall of the capital: "After the fall of Tripoli to forces of the opposition NTC in August 2011, Gaddafi and his family escaped the Libyan capital... In fact, Gaddafi had fled in a small convoy to Sirte on the day Tripoli fell", and it was at Sirte, two months later, that he was caught and killed. The Tripoli article says the same thing from its own end: the battle was the National Transitional Council "attempting to overthrow Gaddafi and take control of the capital". `precondition-of` and not `caused`: losing the capital is what put him in the town where he died, and the article argues no more than that. `probable` because both citations are Wikipedia (rule 22).
explanations.bpn-nationalisation-2008--troika-bailout: The rescue put a large and, for years, uncertain liability onto the public accounts at the moment when the market was pricing Portuguese debt on exactly such uncertainties. It is one of the specific reasons the numbers looked worse in 2011 than they had in 2008.
explanations.chadian-intervention-in-northern-mali--b: The battle was fought by two columns and one of them was Chad's: "France was also seeking the help of Chad's President Idriss Déby. He agreed to deploy his army in the Adrar of Ifoghas. On February 3, the first Chadian soldiers arrived in Kidal." The article's own account of the fighting has the valley "caught between two armored columns, one French to the west and another Chadian to the east". The Chadian article says it from its side: on 22 February "the Chadian army launched a joint military operation with the support of French war jets on an Islamists base said to be of 'significant importance' ... hidden in the mountains of the Adrar des Ifoghas". Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.colombian-peace-process--catatumbo-campa: The campaign’s own lead places it after the accord in one clause: it "is an extension of the war on drugs and developed after the Colombian peace process of 2016." That is as far as the article goes — it names the accord as what the campaign developed after and argues no mechanism for it, so the weakest of the five types is the honest one here and the confidence is `probable`. `enabled` says the earlier record made room for the later, not that it brought it about; what the source states is the sequence and the reader can see where the argument stops. Rule 22 would refuse `consensus` on a Wikipedia citation in any case.
explanations.comprehensive-peace-agreement--2011-sout: The English article on the Comprehensive Peace Agreement says that it set a timetable for a Southern Sudanese independence referendum. The vote of January 2011 is the one the accord scheduled.
explanations.costa-resigns-2023--legislative-election: The resignation left a majority government without the prime minister it had been built around, and the president chose dissolution over a replacement from the same benches. The election of March 2024 is the direct consequence of that choice, and its date was set within a week of the resignation.
explanations.covid-19-pandemic--covid-19-pandemic-in-: The European epidemic is the same epidemic: the first confirmed cases on the continent, in France on 24 January 2020, were travellers from Wuhan, and the northern Italian cluster of February is what turned importation into transmission across the continent. The atlas keeps the two as separate events because the Portuguese chain runs through the European one and not through the Chinese one — what closed Portugal in March 2020 was an epidemic already inside Europe and inside Spain.

The American article opens on the outbreak this atlas dates from Wuhan and then on its arrival: "On 31 December 2019, China announced the discovery of a cluster of pneumonia cases in Wuhan. The first American case of COVID-19 was reported on January 20, and Health and Human Services Secretary Alex Azar declared a public health emergency on January 31." Caused and not enabled: it is the same epidemic, reported twenty days later in another country. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.covid-19-pandemic-in-europe--covid-19-pa: The Brazilian article names the journey the first case came off: "The virus was confirmed to have spread to Brazil on 25 February 2020, when a man from São Paulo who had traveled to Italy tested positive for the virus." Caused: the article makes the Italian epidemic the source of the first Brazilian case, and Italy is inside the record this edge runs from. Probable: Wikipedia alone.

The Chilean article says where the first cases came from: "The virus was confirmed to have reached Chile on 3 March 2020. Initial cases had been imported from Southeast Asia and Europe, and expanded into a large number of untraceable infections." Caused, and partly: the article names Europe as one of two sources and this atlas holds only the European one. Probable: Wikipedia alone, and the article divides the origin between two continents.

The Peruvian article names the journey: "The virus spread to Peru on 6 March 2020, when a 25-year-old man who had travelled to Spain, France, and the Czech Republic tested positive." Caused, on the article's own account of the index case; all three countries it names are inside the record this edge runs from. Probable: Wikipedia alone.

The continental article dates the arrival to one case: "The COVID-19 pandemic was confirmed to have reached South America on 26 February 2020 when Brazil confirmed a case in São Paulo." The Brazilian article says where that case had been: "a man from São Paulo who had traveled to Italy tested positive for the virus." Caused, on the article's own account of the index case, and not a claim about the whole continent. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.covid-19-pandemic-in-europe--covid-state: Portugal confirmed its first cases on 2 March 2020, closed the schools on the 16th and had a state of emergency declared on the 18th — the first under the constitution of 1976 — with the epidemic in Spain a fortnight ahead of its own and Italy's hospitals already overwhelmed. The decision was taken on what was happening in Europe rather than on what had yet happened here: the Portuguese curve at the moment of the declaration was small, and the argument made for the measures was explicitly that Italy and Spain showed what the following fortnight would look like.
explanations.covid-19-pandemic-in-the-united-states--: The Guyanese article names where its first case had travelled from: "The virus was confirmed to have reached Guyana on 11 March 2020. The first case was a woman who travelled from New York, a 52-year-old woman with underlying health conditions." Caused, on the article's own account of that one case. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.covid-state-of-emergency-2020--marcelo-r: The presidential election of January 2021 was held in the worst weeks of the winter wave, under the restrictions the emergency had normalised, with campaigning curtailed and turnout below forty per cent. A first-round win against a divided field owed something to a contest nobody was able to fight in the ordinary way.
explanations.covid-state-of-emergency-2020--world-you: Lisbon had been given the celebration for 2022. The pandemic that the state of emergency marks in Portugal is why it was held in August 2023 instead, and why it was planned twice. The edge is about the postponement and about nothing else.
explanations.crisis-portugal--2011-portuguese-legisla: The ballot of 5 June 2011 was early and it was about the crisis: the fourth austerity package was voted down in March, José Sócrates resigned, and the country voted six weeks after the request for assistance, under a memorandum the two largest opposition parties had already signed. Probable rather than settled because an early election always has more than one proximate cause — the arithmetic of the minority government returned in 2009 is the other, and the atlas already draws that line to the bailout rather than here.
explanations.crisis-portugal--troika-bailout-2011--ca: The request of 6 April 2011 is what the crisis produced. By the spring of 2011 the state could not repay or refinance its debt on the market at a rate the treasury could carry; parliament had rejected the fourth austerity package, the government had resigned, and the memorandum with the Commission, the European Central Bank and the Fund was signed six weeks later. The direction is not in question and the record at the other end says the same thing from its own side. What is argued about is the composition of the crisis rather than this link, and the atlas puts that argument on the edge from the euro.
explanations.euromaidan--2014-pro-russian-unrest-in-u: The unrest’s own lead dates it from Euromaidan’s outcome and names that outcome — the ousting of Yanukovych — as what the demonstrations were against. The article reads: "From the end of February 2014, in the aftermath of the Euromaidan and the Revolution of Dignity, which resulted in the ousting of Russian-leaning Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych, demonstrations by Russian-backed, pro-Russian, and anti-government groups (as well as pro-government demonstrations) took place in Crimea, Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, and Odesa."
explanations.euromaidan--russo-ukrainian-war--caused: The soldiers without insignia appeared in Crimea on 27 February 2014, five days after Yanukovych left Kyiv, and the sequence is not in doubt: Russia acted when the government it had just spent a winter defending fell, and its stated justification was that what had happened in Kyiv was a coup against a legitimate president and a threat to Russian speakers. The claim is about the occasion and the justification. Whether the annexation was an improvisation or the execution of a plan the crisis merely brought forward is argued, and this edge does not settle it.
explanations.fall-of-kabul-2021--republican-insurgenc: The article's §Panjshir conflict: "With the fall of Kabul, former Northern Alliance members and other anti-Taliban forces based in the province Panjshir, led by Ahmad Massoud and former vice president Amrullah Saleh, became the primary organized resistance to the Taliban in Afghanistan." The resistance the article describes is what this atlas holds as `republican-insurgency-in-afghanistan`, and the article dates the change to the fall itself. The atlas already carries `war-in-afghanistan-2001-2021 --caused--> republican-insurgency-in-afghanistan`; this is the same claim at the grain of the single day the article says turned those forces into an insurgency, which is the shape batch 43 wrote for the invasion of Iraq beside the war. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.first-battle-of-benghazi--second-battle-: The first article, § End: "The compound was taken by opposition forces hours later ... However, Younis defected to the opposition and granted safe passage to Gaddafi's loyalists out of the city. Gaddafi's troops evacuated". The second article opens on the consequence of that, a city the government no longer held: the battle of 19-20 March was fought "between army units and militiamen loyal to Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, and anti-Gaddafi forces in Benghazi". `precondition-of` and not `caused`: February is why Benghazi was a rebel city in March, which is the condition of the second battle and not its cause — the atlas is joining two statements here rather than repeating one, which is what keeps this at probable.
explanations.first-battle-of-brega--battle-of-ras-lan: Brega's own article states where the losing side went and what the winning side did next: "The government force retreated to Ra's Lanuf, about 120 km west of Brega, after the battle", and, in § Aftermath, "On 4 March, anti-Gaddafi fighters launched an attack against Ra's Lanuf." Ras Lanuf's article says the same from the other end: "The first phase of confrontation followed two days after the First Battle of Brega which occurred in the town Brega, roughly 130 kilometres (81 mi) to the east of Ras Lanuf." `precondition-of` and not `caused`: what Brega gave the next battle is where both armies then were, which is a position and not a motive. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.first-gulf-of-sidra-offensive--third-bat: The third battle's § Background is an account of the offensive collapsing back onto Brega: "After advancing rapidly along the coast of the Gulf of Sidra in a previous offensive, the rebels were quickly pushed back. They had initially advanced 300 kilometres (190 miles) from Ajdabiya to just 120 kilometres (75 miles) from Gaddafi's hometown of Sirte. However, they were forced to retreat in a government counter-offensive and by 30 March, were back to their starting positions at Ajdabiya, with Brega being retaken by the loyalists that night." The battle this atlas dates from 31 March is the counter-attack on the town retaken that night. `precondition-of`: the offensive's failure is what put Brega back in loyalist hands to be fought over. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.fourth-battle-of-brega--battle-of-sirte-: The fourth battle's article ends in a section called "Rebel advance on Sirte" and states where the front went: "A spokesman for the National Liberation Army said on 22 August that Gaddafi's forces had finally retreated westward to Sirte and all of Brega was under the opposition's control", and then "rebel forces managed to capture village of El Agheila and were on their way to Ra's Lanuf. Ra's Lanuf fell to the opposition soon after and they were on the outskirts of the small town of Bin Jawad, just east of Gaddafi's home town of Sirte." The eastern front the battle unblocked is the one that reached Sirte on 15 September. `precondition-of`: it opened the road, and the article claims nothing more than that. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.fourth-battle-of-gao--battle-of-imenas--: The Imenas article's background gives the failed raids on Gao as the reason for the operation it is about: after the attempts of 10 and 20 February "failed", "French and Malian forces, wished to secure the region, and fully expel the MUJAO-Mulathamen coalition from the Gao and its regions, so they began interrogating captured jihadists to learn information about the positions and the number of the jihadists", and out of that intelligence "French code-named Operation Doro was launched on 27 February, with the aim of destroying Islamist groups around Gao." The article states a purpose and the prisoners it was built on, not only the order of two dates. The link is written from the later of the two raids, which is the one the operation followed. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.full-scale-russo-ukrainian-war--bucha-ma: Bucha was occupied because it lies on the road from Belarus to Kyiv, which is the axis of the attempt to take the capital in the first days of the invasion, and the killings were done during that occupation and found when the column withdrew at the end of March. The claim is about the occasion and nothing more: what a Russian army was doing in a commuter town thirty kilometres from Kyiv is answered entirely by the plan of 24 February. Whether the killings were ordered, tolerated or done by units out of control is a question of command responsibility that this edge does not decide.
explanations.full-scale-russo-ukrainian-war--wagner-g: The mutiny of June 2023 came out of a quarrel about the conduct of one war: Wagner had been given the assault on Bakhmut, had recruited tens of thousands of convicts to do it, and Prigozhin spent the spring accusing the Ministry of Defence of starving his men of ammunition. The order to bring private companies under ministry contracts, which would have ended Wagner as a separate army, is what he moved against. Without the war there is no force of that size under a private command and no quarrel over its supply.
explanations.gaza-war--gaza-genocide--caused: The two records describe the same eighteen months from different positions: one is the war, the other is the finding that the way it has been fought amounts to the destruction of a people as such. The edge exists because the atlas holds both and a reader is owed the relation between them; it is marked disputed because that relation is the thing in dispute, and this project's worst available mistake would be to present either side of it as settled. What is not in dispute and is not the subject of this edge: the scale of the killing, the destruction of the housing, hospitals and universities of the Strip, and the displacement of nearly its whole population.
explanations.gaza-war--twelve-day-war--precondition-o: The war of June 2025 is the last step of a regional escalation that began on 8 October 2023, when Hezbollah opened the northern front, and ran through the Houthi campaign in the Red Sea, the killing of Iranian officers in Damascus, and the two direct exchanges of missiles between Iran and Israel in April and October 2024 — the first in the history of either state. By 2025 Iran's allies had been broken and its air defences opened, which is the condition of a surprise attack on the nuclear sites. The immediate cause was the nuclear programme and the negotiation that had stalled over it; what the Gaza war supplied was the sequence that made a direct war between the two states ordinary.
explanations.geringonca-2015--legislative-election-20: The PS returned in 2019 with more votes than in 2015, and the four years of the arrangement are the usual explanation: incomes recovered, the government held its term, and the parties that had supported it did not bring it down before the end.

The election of January 2022 was called because the arrangement of 2015 had ended: the two parties that had kept the PS in office voted its budget down, and the president dissolved parliament rather than let a government continue without one. The arrangement is therefore a precondition of the election in the strict sense — the election happened at that moment because the arrangement had existed and had stopped.
explanations.geringonca-2015--marcelo-elected-preside: The presidential campaign ran through the new government's first weeks, and the winner made cohabitation with it the substance of his candidacy rather than an afterthought, which is what allowed a candidate of the defeated side to win in the first round. A different government in November would have produced a different January.
explanations.government-falls-2025--legislative-elect: A government defeated on a motion of confidence resigns, and with no alternative majority available in the same chamber the president dissolved parliament rather than look for one. The poll of 18 May follows from the vote of 11 March with nothing between them but the campaign.
explanations.iraq-war--iraqi-insurgency--caused: The insurgency’s article ties both of its ends to the war: it “lasted from 2003 until 2011, beginning shortly after the 2003 American invasion deposed longtime leader Saddam Hussein, and lasting until the end of the Iraq War and U.S. withdrawal in 2011”. The invasion is the event this atlas holds as `iraq-war`.
explanations.iraqi-insurgency--iraqi-civil-war-of-200: The civil war’s article names the insurgency as the thing that became it, and the day it did: “In February 2006, the insurgency against the coalition and government escalated into a sectarian civil war after the bombing of Al-Askari Shrine, considered a holy site in Twelver Shi’ism.” One conflict escalating into another is what `caused` is for here. The confidence is `probable` and not `consensus` because the only citation is an encyclopedia article, which is rule 22.
explanations.kidal-offensive--abeibara-massacres--pre: The massacres' own § Background makes the offensive what put the CSP-PSD in Abeïbara: "Malian and Wagner forces launched an offensive on the Tuareg rebel capital of Kidal, capturing it in November 2023. Remaining CSP-PSD fighters fled to the rural towns of Abeïbara, Tinzaouaten, and the Adrar des Ifoghas mountains." The June 2024 operation went after them there — "Their convoys left the towns of Kidal and Tessalit, and settled in Imaswaqassen, a village four kilometers from Abeibara" — and the killings were the reprisals around it. Precondition and not cause: the article says the offensive made Abeïbara the ground, not that it ordered what was done there. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.kidal-offensive--battle-of-tinzaouaten-2: One sentence of the Abeïbara article names Tinzaouaten for the same reason it names Abeïbara: after the Malian and Wagner offensive "on the Tuareg rebel capital of Kidal, capturing it in November 2023", the "Remaining CSP-PSD fighters fled to the rural towns of Abeïbara, Tinzaouaten, and the Adrar des Ifoghas mountains." The battle's own § Prelude is that column arriving: on 20 July 2024 a FAMa and Wagner convoy "engaged in a series of search operations in northern Mali, mainly looking for Tuareg rebels who held territory in the strongholds of Inafarak and Tinzaouten." Precondition and not cause: the offensive is why the CSP was at Tinzaouaten and why the convoy went there, and neither article says it caused the ambush. Probable: Wikipedia alone, and the first of the two articles is the one that states the link.
explanations.legislative-election-2015--geringonca-20: The election produced a chamber in which the largest list had no majority and the parties to its left had one between them. That arithmetic, and not any prior intention — the PS had campaigned against exactly such an arrangement — is what made a minority government supported from outside by the Bloco de Esquerda and the PCP possible for the first time since 1974.
explanations.legislative-election-2019--legislative-e: The government elected in 2019 governed without renewing the written agreements of 2015 and fell when the budget for 2022 was rejected by the same parties it had stopped writing agreements with. The second election follows from the terms on which the first government was formed rather than from any single vote.
explanations.legislative-election-2022--2022-portugue: Rio had led the party into two legislative elections and lost both, the second to the first absolute majority any party had won since 2005, and he did not stand again. The leadership ballot of 28 May follows from that defeat as directly as the Socialist ballot of July 2011 followed from theirs: the contest existed because the leader who had just lost would not be the leader at the next election.
explanations.legislative-election-2022--costa-resigns: An absolute majority meant that the prime minister could not be forced out by any vote in the chamber, so his going could only be his own act; it also meant that when he went, the majority was left without the person it had been assembled around. Both halves of that follow from the result of January 2022 rather than from the inquiry.
explanations.legislative-election-2022--legislative-e: The majority elected in January 2022 did not last two years, and the election of March 2024 is where its collapse was settled: the same electorate, two years later, returned a chamber in which the PS was no longer the largest list and a party founded in 2019 held fifty seats.
explanations.legislative-election-2024--montenegro-go: The Aliança Democrática was the largest list and the only formation able to govern without Chega, whose support the winner had refused during the campaign and refused again after it. The minority government appointed on 2 April is what that refusal and that arithmetic left available.
explanations.libyan-civil-war--2011-military-interven: Read in this direction the edge says the intervention was the answer to the war. The article's first sentence: "On 19 March 2011, a NATO-led coalition began a military intervention into the ongoing Libyan Civil War to implement United Nations Security Council Resolution 1973", a resolution passed "with the stated intent to have 'an immediate ceasefire in Libya, including an end to the current attacks against civilians, which it said might constitute crimes against humanity'". The war is what was reacted to and the resolution is the form the reaction took; the coalition had no quarrel with Libya before the attacks on civilians the resolution names. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.libyan-civil-war--2012-malian-coup-d-eta: The coup’s own background makes the Libyan war the supply: the men and the weapons that made the Tuareg rebellion winnable came back from it, and the army’s failure against that rebellion is what the officers mutinied over. The article reads: "The Tuareg rebels had been bolstered by an influx of battle-hardened, well-armed fighters returning from the Libyan Civil War, to which they had traveled to fight for Muammar Gaddafi, the Libyan leader who was deposed and killed."
explanations.libyan-civil-war--2012-tuareg-rebellion-: The rebellion’s article says where its fighters and their weapons came from: “The MNLA was formed by former insurgents and a significant number of heavily armed Tuaregs who fought in the Libyan Civil War.” `enabled`, because the Tuareg claim on Azawad is older — the same sentence calls the rising “part of a series of insurgencies by traditionally nomadic Tuaregs which date back at least to 1916” — and what Libya supplied was the men and the arms.
explanations.libyan-civil-war--mali-war--precondition: The English article says that from February 2011, with the collapse of Gaddafi's Libya, hundreds of his Tuareg fighters — many veterans of earlier rebellions and now unemployed — returned to Mali with large stockpiles of weapons, and that in October 2011 the returning fighters negotiated at Zakak with local leaders and formed the National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad, which began the rebellion of 16 January 2012. The article hangs that sentence on Miroiu and Alecu, so two authors and not one encyclopedia stand behind it.
explanations.libyan-civil-war--operation-odyssey-dawn: Read in this direction the edge says the operation was the answer to the war. The article's first sentences: it was "the U.S. code name for the American role in the international military operation in Libya to enforce United Nations Security Council Resolution 1973", and "The initial operation implemented a no-fly zone that was proposed during the Libyan Civil War to prevent government forces loyal to Muammar Gaddafi from carrying out air attacks on anti-Gaddafi forces." The war is what was reacted to and the no-fly zone is the form the reaction took. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.mahsa-amini-protests--2025-2026-iranian-: The protests of 2022 and 2023 changed no leadership and left the government more firmly in place, which is what the record of them says; what they left was a repertoire, a slogan and a demonstration of how far the thing could be pushed and where it stopped. The claim is narrow and it is about inheritance rather than cause: the later protests are of the same kind and draw on the earlier, and the atlas is careful not to say more than that about an unfinished sequence.
explanations.mali-war--2020-malian-coup-d-etat--cause: The coup’s article gives the protests behind it and what the protesters were angry about: “Protests in Mali had been ongoing since 5 June, with protesters calling for the resignation of President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. Protesters were displeased with the government’s management of the ongoing insurgency, alleged government corruption, the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, and a floundering economy.” The insurgency is the war this edge runs from; it is **one of four** grievances the article names, which is exactly why this is `probable` and why no edge is written from the other three.
explanations.marcelo-elected-president-2016--marcelo-: The English article on the election of 2021 describes it as the re-election of a sitting president: the incumbent, Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, was re-elected for a second term, by a landslide of 60.7 per cent, winning every district and all 308 municipalities.
explanations.montenegro-government-2024--government-f: A minority government that had ruled out the only party able to give it a majority had no way of answering questions about the prime minister's family company except by asking the chamber to confirm it. The chamber did not, and the motion the government lost was its own: the fall follows from the terms on which it had taken office eleven months earlier.
explanations.operation-car-wash-2014--lula-returns-to: The same inquiry that barred him is what he came back through. A series of Supreme Federal Court rulings questioning the legality of his trial and the impartiality of the judge released him from prison in 2019, annulled Moro’s cases against him, and restored his political rights by 2021 — which is what made the candidacy of 2022 possible at all.
explanations.operation-car-wash-2014--the-2018-brazil: The inquiry decided who could stand. Lula intended to run and led the polling for both rounds; his 2017 conviction on corruption charges barred him, and on 1 September 2018 the Superior Electoral Court rejected his candidacy six to one under the Ficha Limpa law. The Workers’ Party replaced him with Fernando Haddad, then largely unknown to the electorate, who lost the runoff to Jair Bolsonaro.
explanations.operation-car-wash-2014--the-impeachment: The petition accused the president of criminal responsibility for failing to act on the scandal at Petrobras that Car Wash had uncovered, and for failing to distance herself from those under investigation; she had chaired the Petrobras board during the period investigated. The Petrobras charges were finally left out of the trial, on the prosecutor-general’s argument that a sitting president could not be investigated for acts before election — which is why this is `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the inquiry set the terms of the crisis without supplying the article she was tried under.
explanations.operation-jaque--colombian-peace-process: The peace process’s own background dates the first discreet contacts with the FARC from the month of the rescue. The article reads: "In July 2008, following the successful rescue of 15 hostages by the Colombian military during Operation Jaque, the government initiated discreet contacts with the FARC."
explanations.operation-odyssey-dawn--operation-unifie: The article: "The operation began with a naval arms embargo, while command of the no-fly zone and the air strikes against Libyan Armed Forces remained under command of the international coalition, led by France, the United Kingdom and the United States ... On 24 March NATO decided to take control of the no-fly zone enforcement, by integrating the air assets of the international coalition under NATO command ... formal transfer of command occurred at 06:00 GMT on 31 March 2011, formally ending the national operations such as the U.S.-coordinated Operation Odyssey Dawn." It adds that "The no-fly zone was enforced by aircraft transferred to Unified Protector from the international coalition". `precondition-of` and not `caused`: what the coalition operation gave the NATO one is the no-fly zone, the command and the aircraft it took over, which is a thing that had to be in place rather than a motive. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.operation-serval--battle-of-diabaly--rea: Diabaly's § Background makes the battle an answer to the French air campaign: "On 13 January, the French Air Force bombarded major Islamist towns throughout northern Mali. As a result of this hundreds of Islamists fled to the Mauritania border, where they launched a counterattack on the western town of Diabaly." The atlas's reacted-to runs forward in time: Diabaly answered Serval. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.operation-serval--operation-barkhane--pr: The English article on Operation Barkhane says that following the end of Operation Serval France recognised the need to provide stability in the wider Sahel region, that Barkhane was launched for that purpose, and that the operation is the successor of Operation Serval and of Operation Epervier in Chad.
explanations.operation-unified-protector--battle-of-t: The article, § Operation Mermaid Dawn plans and aims: "The plan was discussed between the NTC and the French government, and rebels drew up a list of over 120 targets for NATO to strike, although the actual number of targets struck was much lower. Memory cards containing information on loyalist command and control centres and other regime military and intelligence facilities were supplied to NATO by rebel cells in Tripoli." The assault was planned around the NATO air campaign, which by 21 August had been Unified Protector for five months. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article has the strikes as something the plan was built on and counted on, not as the reason anyone attacked. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.orange-revolution--euromaidan--precondit: Euromaidan is the same square, over the same question of which way the country faces, against the same politician. What 2004 established was the repertoire — the permanent occupation of Independence Square as the way a Ukrainian government is challenged — and what it failed to establish is the reason the repertoire was needed again: the constitutional and anti-corruption settlement of 2005 did not hold, and Yanukovych returned to the presidency by election in 2010. The claim is about the precedent and the unfinished business, not that 2004 caused 2013, whose trigger was the association agreement and Russian pressure against it.
explanations.pedrogao-grande-fires-2017--october-fire: The failures the Independent Technical Commission found in June — the alert, the closing of the roads, the emergency communications network — had not been repaired by 15 October, and the second wave met the same system with the same gaps. This is a claim about what was not done in the four months between them, not that one fire lit the other.
explanations.prelude-to-the-russian-invasion-of-ukrai: The article is the build-up and it ends on the invasion: "On the morning of 24 February, Putin announced that Russia was initiating a \"special military operation\" in the Donbas, and launched a full-scale invasion into Ukraine", after a year in which "Russia had assembled 83 battalion tactical groups, estimated to be 70 percent of its combat capabilities, for a full-scale invasion of Ukraine". The item says the same thing as a pointer, Q110116635 P156. It is precondition-of and not caused because the article is an account of what was in place before the decision, not an argument that the build-up compelled it; the two records are siblings under russo-ukrainian-war, and this is the edge the filing cannot make.
explanations.raid-on-dioura-2023--kidal-offensive--re: The offensive's own § Prelude counts the raid on Dioura among what it answered: "The CSP-PSD began a series of raids against Malian and Wagner military bases throughout September; Bourem, Léré, Dioura, Bamba, and Taoussa were all pillaged between September 12 and October 3, and dozens of Malian soldiers were killed." The next sentence is the answer — "In response to the attacks, the Malian junta launched airstrikes on Kidal on October 2" — and October 2 is the day the offensive is dated from. Written forward in time, so the raid is the thing reacted to and the offensive is the reaction. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.revolution-of-dignity--2014-pro-russian-: The unrest’s article dates it to the revolution and says what it answered: “From the end of February 2014, in the aftermath of the Euromaidan and the Revolution of Dignity, which resulted in the ousting of Russian-leaning Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych, demonstrations by Russian-backed, pro-Russian, and anti-government groups took place in Crimea, Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, and Odesa.” The same sentence says the unrest “was supported by the Russian military and intelligence services”, so the ousting is the occasion and not the whole cause, which is what `probable` is for.
explanations.revolution-of-dignity--russo-ukrainian-w: The English article's lead says in one sentence that "the revolution prompted Russia to occupy Crimea, starting the Russo-Ukrainian war", and its third paragraph adds that pro-Russian counter-revolutionary protests began in parts of south-eastern Ukraine, that Russia occupied and then annexed Crimea, and that armed Russian-backed separatists seized government buildings and proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk, sparking the Donbas war.
explanations.rose-revolution--orange-revolution--insp: The English article on the Georgian revolution says plainly that the Orange Revolution, which followed the disputed Ukrainian presidential election of November 2004, "is said to have been partly inspired by the Georgian Rose Revolution". The article on the Ukrainian one carries the contemporary version of the same observation, an editorial of February 2004 arguing that Ukraine offered the best chance to build on the Georgian success and that the democratic opposition’s actions were inspired by Georgia and Serbia. The type is `inspired` because that is the whole of the claim: example and not cause.
explanations.rose-revolution--tulip-revolution--inspi: The English article names the transmission and the man who carried it: “Givi Targamadze, a former member of the Liberty Institute of Georgia and the chair of Georgian Parliamentary Committee on Defense and Security, consulted Ukrainian opposition leaders on the technique of nonviolent struggle. He later advised leaders of the Kyrgyz opposition during the Tulip Revolution.” The same section records that the name itself was chosen against the Georgian and Ukrainian precedents, Akayev having warned that no such “Color Revolution” should happen in Kyrgyzstan. Inspired and not caused: what crossed was a technique and a name.
explanations.russo-georgian-war--russo-ukrainian-war-: What happened in Georgia in 2008 was done again in Ukraine in 2014 in the same order: a separatist territory supported and then garrisoned, a passportisation of its residents that supplied a protection claim, a rapid operation the West was not prepared for, and a recognition of the result that nobody was going to reverse. The four months of Western sanction that followed 2008 lapsed and the reset with Moscow was under way within a year. The claim is that the precedent and its cost were both established in 2008; the causes of 2014 are in Ukraine, and this edge does not reach for them.
explanations.russo-ukrainian-war--full-scale-russo-uk: The invasion of February 2022 is not the beginning of a war but a decision to end by force what eight years of the existing one had failed to settle. The Minsk agreements had committed Ukraine to a constitutional status for the occupied districts that no Ukrainian parliament would pass and Russia to a withdrawal it never made, so the front line froze and the political instrument for changing it was exhausted; Moscow recognised the two republics as states on 21 February 2022 and invaded three days later. The claim is that the earlier war supplied the stalemate, the pretext and the recognised entities the invasion was launched to protect.
explanations.second-battle-of-brega--battle-of-ajdabi: Ajdabiya's article states what the second battle of Brega left in front of it: "Following the Second Battle of Brega, in which pro-Gaddafi forces captured the town, Ajdabiya was the only major rebel-held city left en route to the rebel capital of Benghazi." `precondition-of`: losing Brega is what made Ajdabiya the next thing on the road, which is a position on a coastal highway and not a cause. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.second-battle-of-gao--fourth-battle-of-g: The same sentence of the Imenas article names two attempts and not one: after the capture of Gao on 27 January the jihadists who stayed in the region "tried to take back the city, in two attempted operations before, first on 10 February, and then again on 20 February, but their attacks failed", with "20 February" linked to the fourth battle. The atlas already holds the third as the fourth's precondition, so this edge adds no path the graph did not have; it is here because the article states the answer twice and the second statement is about this record.
explanations.second-battle-of-gao--third-battle-of-ga: Neither Gao article names the other, and a third one does it for them. The Imenas article's background states the capture and the answer to it in one sentence: "Gao was captured by French and Malian troops on 27 January 2013, about a month before this battle. However, unlike Ansar Dine and Al-Qaeda in Islamic Maghreb, which retreated to the Adrar des Ifoghas, the Movement for Oneness and Jihad in West Africa and Mulathamen remained in the Gao region. They tried to take back the city, in two attempted operations before, first on 10 February, and then again on 20 February, but their attacks failed." The article links "10 February" to the third battle and "captured" to the second, so the pairing is the article's own and not this atlas's reading. Written in the direction the edge vocabulary takes: the capture is what was answered, the raid is the answer. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.second-intifada--gaza-war--precondition-: The English article on the Gaza war writes its background as the Israeli–Palestinian conflict and names the two uprisings within it: the First and Second Intifadas of 1987 and 2000, with the latter’s end seeing Israel’s unilateral withdrawal from Gaza in 2005. The withdrawal that left the territory the later war was fought over is what the article says the intifada’s end brought.
explanations.second-intifada--gaza-war-2008-2009--pre: The English article on the war of 2008–2009 opens its background with the intifada’s end: on 8 February 2005 Mahmoud Abbas and Ariel Sharon signed a ceasefire agreement to bring an end to the Second Intifada, and on 17 March the thirteen main Palestinian factions agreed to it conditional on a cessation of Israeli attacks; Israel completed its unilateral disengagement from Gaza in September 2005. The article then dates the breakdown of that ceasefire to June 2006.
explanations.siege-of-tessalit--tinsalane-ambush--pre: The ambush's own lead makes the siege the reason the convoy was on that road: the rebels "fought against a convoy of the Malian army who came to reinforce the troops besieged in Tessalit". § The ambush says the same twice over — "On February 10, 2012, the Malian army launched an offensive to rescue the garrison of Amachach camp, near Tessalit, besieged by the rebels", and "a convoy of Malian soldiers and militia departed the cities of Kidal and Anfif and moved towards Tessalit to strengthen the military forces of the besieged city. However, this convoy was ambushed by an MNLA brigade in Tinsalane." Precondition and not cause: the siege produced the relief column the ambush destroyed, and the article does not say the besiegers ordered the ambush. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.the-2018-brazilian-general-election--202: The English article introduces the 2022 contest as the 2018 one still being settled: Bolsonaro "had been elected in 2018 as the candidate of the Social Liberal Party but left that party in 2019", and "Lula's intended candidacy in 2018 was disallowed due to his conviction on corruption charges in 2017 and subsequent arrest; a series of court rulings led to his release from prison in 2019, followed by the annulment of his conviction and restoration of his political rights by 2021." The two candidates of 2022 are the winner of 2018 and the man kept off that ballot.
explanations.the-2018-brazilian-general-election--lul: The 2022 election was a rematch and is read as one: the incumbent seeking a second term against the man the courts had kept off the ballot four years earlier. Lula won the runoff 50.90 to 49.10 per cent, the first person elected president of Brazil three times, and Bolsonaro became the first incumbent since the re-election amendment of 1997 not to be returned.
explanations.the-commodity-boom-and-the-chinese-buyer: The president was impeached in the recession that followed the boom. She began her second term weakened by the Brazilian economic recession of 2014–2016 as well as by the corruption allegations, and her disapproval reached 71 per cent — the highest for any president since redemocratisation. The supercycle had peaked in 2011. An economy organised around selling commodities is an economy whose politics turns when the price does, which is the thesis of this whole walk stated once more at the end of it.
explanations.the-impeachment-of-dilma-rousseff-2016--: The election was fought on what the impeachment left. Temer, who replaced Rousseff, broke sharply with her policies, amended the constitution to freeze public spending, reached an approval rating of 7 per cent against 76 per cent wanting him gone, and was himself ineligible to stand. A right-wing outsider won an election in which the party that had governed since 2002 could field neither its president nor its strongest candidate.
explanations.third-battle-of-gao--fourth-battle-of-ga: The fourth battle's article opens its account by naming the third and the relation between them: "Ten days after the Third Battle of Gao, the Jihadists launched another offensive to retake the city on 20 February 2013." Both leads say the same thing from either side — the third was "a raid on the city" whose "raiders were defeated", the fourth "an attempt by rebel MOJWA forces to retake the city" — so the sentence is stating a second attempt by the same force at the same objective and not only a date. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.treaty-establishing-a-constitution-for-e: The Lisbon treaty is what the constitutional treaty’s failure produced. The English article says the negotiations begun in 2001 resulted first in the proposed constitution, which was abandoned after rejection by 55% of French voters on 29 May 2005 and 61% of Dutch voters on 1 June; that after "a period of reflection" the member states agreed instead to keep the existing treaties and amend them, "to bring into law a number of the reforms that had been envisaged in the abandoned constitution"; and that the amending reform treaty was drawn up and signed at Lisbon in 2007. The constitutional treaty’s own article says the same from its end.
explanations.treaty-of-nice--treaty-establishing-a-co: The English article on the treaty that replaced it draws the line from Nice: "The need to review the EU’s constitutional framework, particularly in light of the accession of ten new Member States in 2004, was highlighted in a declaration annexed to the Treaty of Nice in 2001", and the agreements at Nice "had paved the way for further enlargement of the Union by reforming voting procedures". The Laeken declaration of December 2001 followed and set out the process by which a constitution was to be drafted. What is claimed is that Nice left the question open and named it, not that Nice caused the constitutional treaty.
explanations.troika-bailout-2011--bes-resolution-2014: The resolution was carried out under the supervisory regime the 2011 programme had imposed and paid for out of the bank solvency support line the programme had provided. Without that money and that framework the Banco de Portugal would have had to choose between a rescue it could not fund and a disorderly failure; whether the same programme also delayed the recognition of the group's losses is a separate argument this edge does not make.
explanations.troika-bailout-2011--troika-programme-en: The programme signed in May 2011 was written to run for three years, and the exit of May 2014 is that term reached rather than a separate decision. What was decided was the manner of it: the government left without the precautionary line the lenders had prepared, and the IMF's own evaluation records that choice as contested at the time.
explanations.troika-programme-ends-2014--legislative-: The coalition went to the polls seventeen months after the exit and made it the case for its own continuation, so the campaign was fought on whether the adjustment had worked. The result — the most votes and no majority — is the answer the electorate gave to that case, and it is why the arithmetic of the chamber, rather than the size of the largest list, decided what came next.
explanations.tunisian-revolution--2010-2012-algerian-: The article's lead says the protests "were inspired by similar protests across the Middle East and North Africa", and the body names which: "as the widely reported protests sparked off by Mohamed Bouazizi's self-immolation in Tunisia began to have a clear impact on the Tunisian government, a wave of self-immolations swept Algeria", and at the February march "some demonstrators waved the Tunisian flag, alluding to the protests which had brought down Ben Ali". Agence France-Presse is quoted linking the January protests to Tunisia in the same way. An example followed is inspired and not caused, which is the same reading batch 26 gave Bahrain. Probable, for the reason every edge drawn from this source is.
explanations.tunisian-revolution--2011-bahraini-upris: The uprising’s own article names where it came from in its second sentence: “The protests were inspired by the unrest of the 2011 Arab Spring and protests in Tunisia and Egypt and escalated to daily clashes after the Bahraini government repressed the revolt with the support of the Gulf Cooperation Council’s Peninsula Shield Force.” Tunisia is the first of the two it names, and the Arab Spring’s own lead — quoted on the three edges batch 22 wrote — says the wave began there. The type is `inspired` and not `caused` for the same reason as those three: an example spreading is not a Tunisian event bringing about a Bahraini one, and no article this batch read says it was.
explanations.tunisian-revolution--2011-egyptian-revol: The Arab Spring's own article gives the direction of travel and names Egypt among the five: “It began in Tunisia in response to the death of Mohamed Bouazizi by self-immolation. From Tunisia, the protests initially spread to five other countries: Libya, Egypt, Yemen, Syria and Bahrain.” Egypt's article dates its revolution to 25 January 2011, eleven days after Ben Ali left Tunisia, and its lead gives the occasion as National Police Day and the grievance as police brutality — it does not name Tunisia. So what is asserted here is the spread the first article states and not a cause inside Egypt: the type is `inspired` and not `caused`, and the confidence is `probable` because both citations are the same encyclopedia.
explanations.tunisian-revolution--2011-yemeni-revolut: The Arab Spring's article names Yemen among the five countries the protests reached from Tunisia: “It began in Tunisia in response to the death of Mohamed Bouazizi by self-immolation.
